study_type.claude: Mixed methods (metric proposal and validation + controlled experiment + post-hoc case study + counterfactual model)
study_type.nlm: Mixed methods (controlled experiment, case studies, survey, observational UX study, descriptive statistics)
study_type.note: Industrial metric proposal (DAT) with validation and three case studies.

research_method.claude: Telemetry-based metric (DAT) proposal and validation (UX screen-recording study ~20 diffs, survey 968 diffs, descriptive statistics, visualizations); controlled experiment on typed mocking (~10,000 diffs, stratified Welch's t-test); post-hoc React auto-memoization case study (mixed-effects regression, Wasserstein distance); counterfactual code-sharing model (~50,000 diffs)
research_method.nlm: Mixed methods: controlled experiment (typed mocking, ~10,000 diffs), case studies (React n >> 10,000; code sharing ~50,000 diffs), survey (968 diffs), observational UX screen-recording study (~20 diffs), descriptive statistics
research_method.value: Proposal of the telemetry-based Diff Authoring Time (DAT) metric, validated by an observational UX screen-recording study (~20 diffs), a one-question post-diff survey (968 diffs) and descriptive statistics; three case studies: controlled experiment on typed mocking in Hack (~10,000 diffs, two-tailed Welch's t-test), post-hoc case study on React auto-memoization (n >> 10,000 diffs, mixed-effects regression, Wasserstein distance), counterfactual estimation of code-sharing savings (~50,000 diffs)
research_method.note: Welch's t-test reported only by Claude (not contradicted).

context.claude: Industry; Meta (Infrastructure/DevInfra organization), internal tool development; Hack, React, code-sharing frameworks
context.nlm: Industry; Meta Platforms, Inc., DevInfra organization
context.value: industry; Meta Platforms (Infrastructure/DevInfra organization), internal developer tooling (Hack, React, code-sharing frameworks); diff-level samples from ~20 to ~50,000 diffs per study

ai_discussed.note: Claude: only mentions (LLaMA-33B vs 65B as an example diff-level experiment; coding agents may initially worsen DAT; future work). NotebookLM: discusses LLM base models, AI-assisted authoring and coding agents.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not specified by either.

data_window.claude: three weeks in 2024 (typed mocking experiment only)
data_window.note: Only Claude reports a period (three weeks in 2024, typed-mocking experiment); other studies undated.

cat_productivity.note: DAT (active authoring time per diff) is the proposed productivity/velocity metric; TSD also discussed.

cat_quality.note: No quality metric; quality only mentioned as an aspect beyond velocity.

cat_collaboration.note: Review time only cited in related work.

cat_satisfaction.note: Satisfaction mentioned only as an aspect beyond velocity.

cat_activity.note: NotebookLM lists LOC and change count as Activity metrics; Claude treats them as metrics cited in related work. LOC is used only as a covariate (React model) and for size terciles (code sharing).

cat_delivery.note: Thin basis: Code Gestation Time (coding start to diff landing), a predecessor metric superseded by DAT, labelled Delivery by both (NotebookLM also tags DAT as Delivery).

cat_devex.note: DevEx (Fagerholm & Münch; DevEx in Action) and DX Core 4 only referenced.

cat_agile.note: Continuous Experimentation culture, not agile/process metrics.

cat_survey.note: One-question post-diff survey of self-estimated time (968 diffs) used to validate DAT.

evidence.quote: This paper introduces Diff Authoring Time (DAT), a precise, yet conceptually simple approach to measuring software development productivity that enables rigorous experimentation.
We validate DAT through observational studies, surveys, visualizations, and descriptive statistics.
We analyzed n =∼ 20 diffs, achieving an average accuracy of over 90%
Therefore, we conducted a large-scale survey asking developers to estimate the time spent on a diff.
We received responses for 968 unique diffs to compare with DAT values.
To estimate the effect of typed mocking, we employ a two-tailed Welch's t-test, testing on the mean DAT difference between control and test groups.
As a post-hoc case study with non-randomized data, we use the Wasserstein distance to measure the difference between groups.
We initially applied this method to two major code-sharing frameworks, covering thousands of code-sharing diffs and counterfactual diffs monthly
